claims.text: A multiscale ML regression model using ab initio-derived features can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will reduce prediction RMSE by approximately 25% relative to conventional Debye-inspired and DFT-derived analytical approaches.
The model applies to both nominally defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Separate feature sets from phonon density of states, elastic constants, and electronic band structures will decouple lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The proposed applicability range is 50–1200 K and up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Between 300 and 1200 K, HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen has total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m).
Phonon density of states, elastic moduli, and electronic band parameters uniquely govern scattering and transport in their respective channels.
Mapping distinct phonon and electronic descriptors allows the ML model to learn the interdependencies controlling each heat-transport channel.
Separating the channels enables independent validation of lattice and electronic conductivity against temperature-resolved experiments.
Existing models typically conflate lattice and electronic transport through Debye approximations or bulk DFT estimates.
Existing models do not capture relevant atomic-scale complexity and defect effects.
Predictive reliability outside 50–1200 K or above approximately 1 wt.% oxygen is not established.
Low-temperature time-domain thermoreflectance can predominantly isolate phonon-based conduction in HfNbTaTiZr.
High-temperature electrical conductivity and Seebeck measurements, combined with Wiedemann–Franz analysis, can infer the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
Inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering can validate the computed phonon density of states used as model input.
The hypothesis is falsified if separately predicted lattice or electronic conductivity differs from experiment by more than a ±25% margin.

The hypothesis is falsified if the model does not reproduce comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K or total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) for the oxygen-containing sample at high temperature.

contradictions.description: The same 25% figure is used both as a relative reduction in RMSE versus baseline models and as an absolute ±25% prediction-error tolerance. These are different metrics, so the stated improvement does not define or justify the falsification margin.
